quests.instruction: Which three features are heard in “Abel, I’m going to ask her about it”?
quests.word: Abel, I’m going to ask her about it
quests.textToSpeak: Abel, I’m going to ask her about it
options: A contraction, a /dʒ/ blend and gemination, with no linking at all
Elision of a /t/, assimilation of an /n/ and an intrusive /r/ in the line, with nothing linked
A weak “to”, a /ʃ/ blend and a /j/ glide, but no dropped /h/
A reduction (“gonna”), a dropped /h/ with a link (“ask her”), and a linking /t/
quests.correctAnswer: A reduction (“gonna”), a dropped /h/ with a link (“ask her”), and a linking /t/
quests.hint: Take the line from left to right and ask what each boundary triggers.
quests.explanation: “Going to” is reduced to the informal “gonna”. “Her” loses its /h/ and the /k/ of “ask” links onto it: “as-ker”. “About it” has a /t/ before a vowel, so it links: “abou-tit”. Three different features sit in one short line, and each is decided by its own boundary.
quests.phoneticRule: A single line can combine informal reduction, /h/ dropping with linking, and consonant-to-vowel linking, each triggered by its own neighbouring sounds.
quests.spokenForm: Abel, I’m gonna as-ker about it

quests.instruction: Which feature is not heard in “Bruno, get your coat and put it on”?
quests.word: Bruno, get your coat and put it on
quests.textToSpeak: Bruno, get your coat and put it on
options: Gemination, because no two identical consonants meet at a boundary
A /tʃ/ blend in “get your”, because /t/ meets /j/
A reduced “and” after “coat”, because it is unstressed
Linking in “put it on”, because consonants meet vowels
quests.correctAnswer: Gemination, because no two identical consonants meet at a boundary
quests.hint: Check each boundary for the process it could trigger, and find the one that has no trigger.
quests.explanation: “Get your” has /t/ + /j/, so it blends into /tʃ/. “Coat and” has a reduced “and”, /n/. “Put it on” has two consonants before vowels, so it links. But no pair of identical consonants meets anywhere, so there is no gemination. Knowing what is absent is as useful as knowing what is present.
quests.phoneticRule: Each feature needs its own trigger: gemination requires two identical consonants at a boundary, and none occurs in this line.
quests.spokenForm: Bruno, ge-chyer coa-tn pu-ti-ton

quests.instruction: Which spoken form fits “Cora, I’ll tell him I’m on my way”?
quests.word: Cora, I’ll tell him I’m on my way
quests.textToSpeak: Cora, I’ll tell him I’m on my way
options: “tell … him”, two strong words with a pause, and “on my way” unchanged in normal speech here
“tel-chim”, with the /h/ turned into /tʃ/, and “om my way” as well
“te-lim” with a dropped /h/ and a linked /l/, and “om my way” with /n/ shifting to /m/
“te-lim”, but “on” becomes “ong” before “my” in the same breath
quests.correctAnswer: “te-lim” with a dropped /h/ and a linked /l/, and “om my way” with /n/ shifting to /m/
quests.hint: Look at the pronoun first, then at the nasal before “my”.
quests.explanation: “Him” is unstressed after “tell”, so it loses its /h/ and the /l/ links onto it: “te-lim”. In “on my way”, the /n/ sits before the lip sound /m/, so it can shift to [m]: “om my way”. Two earlier stages meet in one sentence.
quests.phoneticRule: A dropped /h/ with linking and place assimilation can co-occur in one sentence, one at each boundary.
quests.spokenForm: Cora, I’ll te-lim I’m om my way

quests.instruction: Which boundary shows assimilation and which shows elision in “Freya, it’s ten past six already”?
quests.word: Freya, it’s ten past six already
quests.textToSpeak: Freya, it’s ten past six already
options: “ten past” shows elision of the /n/; “past six” shows assimilation of the /t/
Both boundaries show assimilation of a nasal to the lips
Both boundaries show elision of a /t/ before a consonant
“ten past”: assimilation (/n/ to [m]); “past six”: elision of the /t/
quests.correctAnswer: “ten past”: assimilation (/n/ to [m]); “past six”: elision of the /t/
quests.hint: Look at what follows each word-final consonant, and whether the sound changes or disappears.
quests.explanation: “Ten” ends in /n/ before the lip sound /p/, so the /n/ shifts to [m]: assimilation. “Past” ends in /st/ before /s/, so the /t/ is often omitted: elision. The same phrase contains one change of place and one omission. Naming each correctly is the point of this level.
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a segment's place to match a neighbour, while elision removes a segment from a crowded cluster; both can occur in one phrase.
quests.spokenForm: Freya, it’s tem pas six already

quests.instruction: In “Greta, the best plan was a great plan”, how do the /t/ sounds in “best plan” and “great plan” differ?
quests.word: Greta, the best plan was a great plan
quests.textToSpeak: Greta, the best plan was a great plan
options: Both /t/ sounds are omitted, because both come before /p/
Both /t/ sounds shift to /p/, because both come before /p/
“best plan”: the /t/ is often omitted (after /s/); “great plan”: it shifts toward /p/
In “best plan” it shifts to /p/ after the /s/; in “great plan” it is omitted after the vowel
quests.correctAnswer: “best plan”: the /t/ is often omitted (after /s/); “great plan”: it shifts toward /p/
quests.hint: Compare the sound before each /t/: a consonant in one, a vowel in the other.
quests.explanation: After /s/ the /t/ sits in a crowded cluster and is often omitted: “bes’ plan”. After a vowel the /t/ is not crowded, so instead of disappearing it takes the lip place of the following /p/: “grayp plan”. The same next sound gives two different outcomes because the preceding sound differs.
quests.phoneticRule: The same following consonant can trigger different processes depending on the sound before the /t/: omission after /s/, assimilation after a vowel.
quests.spokenForm: Greta, the bes’ plan was a grayp plan

quests.instruction: Which spoken form fits “Iris, the old man left a green bag”?
quests.word: Iris, the old man left a green bag
quests.textToSpeak: Iris, the old man left a green bag
options: “ol’ man left a greem bag”: the /d/ is omitted and the /n/ shifts to /m/
“old man left a green bag”: every sound is clearly kept
“ol’ nan left a greeng bag”: the /d/ is omitted and the /m/ shifts to /n/
“ob man left a greeng bag”: the /d/ becomes /b/ and the /n/ shifts to /ŋ/
quests.correctAnswer: “ol’ man left a greem bag”: the /d/ is omitted and the /n/ shifts to /m/
quests.hint: Find the /d/ before a consonant and the nasal before a lip sound.
quests.explanation: The /d/ of “old” sits between /l/ and /m/, so it is often omitted: “ol’ man”. The /n/ of “green” sits before the lip sound /b/, so it can shift to [m]: “greem bag”. One omission and one change of place appear in the same sentence. Telling them apart prevents mixing the two ideas.
quests.phoneticRule: Elision applies to a stop in a crowded cluster, and place assimilation applies to a nasal before a bilabial; both can occur within one sentence.
quests.spokenForm: Iris, the ol’ man left a greem bag

quests.instruction: What is the difference between the weak “you” in “see you” and in “meet you” in “Kiran, see you at eight”?
quests.word: Kiran, see you at eight
quests.textToSpeak: Kiran, see you at eight
options: In both, the weak /jə/ blends with the previous sound into a new consonant sound in fast speech
In “see you” the weak /jə/ takes only a glide; in “meet you” it blends with the /t/ into /tʃ/
In neither is “you” weak, because it is always stressed
In “see you” it blends into /ʒ/, but in “meet you” it does not blend
quests.correctAnswer: In “see you” the weak /jə/ takes only a glide; in “meet you” it blends with the /t/ into /tʃ/
quests.hint: Compare the final sounds of “see” and “meet” and decide which can join the weak “you”.
quests.explanation: The weak /jə/ is the same in both phrases, but what happens next depends on the sound before it. After a vowel (“see”) it takes only a glide: “see-yuh”. After /t/ (“meet”) it blends: “mee-chuh”. So a weak “you” is a necessary condition for a blend, but not a sufficient one.
quests.phoneticRule: A weak “you” triggers coalescence only after /t d s z/; after vowels it merely takes a glide.
quests.spokenForm: Kiran, see-yuh at eight

quests.instruction: Why does the /k/ at the end of “ask” not blend with “you” in “Mina, I’ll ask you later”?
quests.word: Mina, I’ll ask you later
quests.textToSpeak: Mina, I’ll ask you later
options: The /s/ before the /k/ blocks the blend in this cluster
“you” is too weak to cause a blend after any consonant
Only /t/, /d/, /s/ and /z/ blend with /j/; /k/ is not one of them
A /k/ blends with /j/ into /tʃ/ in fast speech
quests.correctAnswer: Only /t/, /d/, /s/ and /z/ blend with /j/; /k/ is not one of them
quests.hint: Think about where in the mouth /k/ is made, compared with /t d s z/.
quests.explanation: Coalescence involves the alveolar stops and fricatives /t d s z/, which are made at the same place as the front of the tongue moves toward /j/. The velar /k/ is made at the back, so it stays separate: “as-kyuh”. So a weak “you” after /k/ keeps a clear /j/.
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescence is limited to the alveolar consonants /t d s z/; velar consonants such as /k/ and /g/ keep a separate /j/.
quests.spokenForm: Mina, I’ll as-kyuh later

quests.instruction: Which junction has a weak /jə/ but no blend in “Nico, I’ll see you and miss you”?
quests.word: Nico, I’ll see you and miss you
quests.textToSpeak: Nico, I’ll see you and miss you
options: “miss you”: “miss” ends in /s/, so there is a glide only
Both junctions blend, because “you” is weak in both
Neither junction has a weak /jə/, because both are stressed and said with a full vowel
“see you”: “see” ends in a vowel, so the weak /jə/ takes only a glide
quests.correctAnswer: “see you”: “see” ends in a vowel, so the weak /jə/ takes only a glide
quests.hint: One first word ends in a vowel, the other in a consonant that can blend.
quests.explanation: “See” ends in a vowel, so the weak “you” takes only a glide: “see-yuh”. “Miss” ends in /s/, so it blends into /ʃ/: “mi-shoo”. The same weak /jə/ follows both words, but only the second junction produces a blend. The first-word sound makes the difference.
quests.phoneticRule: The weak /jə/ blends only when preceded by /t d s z/; after a vowel it is linked with a glide.
quests.spokenForm: Nico, I’ll see-yuh and mi-shoo

quests.instruction: In “Odile, the idea of going far away”, which /r/ is linking and which is intrusive?
quests.word: Odile, the idea of going far away
quests.textToSpeak: Odile, the idea of going far away
options: “idea of” has a linking /r/, and “far away” has an intrusive /r/, as the spelling shows
“far away”: a linking /r/ (spelled “r”); “idea of”: an intrusive /r/ (no “r” spelled)
Both are linking /r/ sounds, because both words end in vowels
Both are intrusive /r/ sounds, because neither is stressed
quests.correctAnswer: “far away”: a linking /r/ (spelled “r”); “idea of”: an intrusive /r/ (no “r” spelled)
quests.hint: Check the spelling of each word before the vowel-initial word.
quests.explanation: “Far” is spelled with a final “r”, so the /r/ before “away” is a linking /r/. “Idea” has no “r” in its spelling, so an /r/ before “of” is intrusive. Both sounds are produced in the same way; the difference is in the spelling. Intrusive /r/ is accent-dependent, and recognising it is the priority.
quests.phoneticRule: A linking /r/ corresponds to a spelled “r”, whereas an intrusive /r/ appears without one, but both are pronounced identically in non-rhotic accents.
quests.spokenForm: Odile, the idea-rof going far-raway

quests.instruction: Which boundaries in “Pablo, the law and the idea are clear” can have an intrusive /r/?
quests.word: Pablo, the law and the idea are clear
quests.textToSpeak: Pablo, the law and the idea are clear
options: “the law” and “the idea”, because “the” precedes both
“and the”, because “and” ends in /d/
“law and” and “idea are”, because /ɔː/ and /ə/ precede vowels
None, because no spelled “r” appears
quests.correctAnswer: “law and” and “idea are”, because /ɔː/ and /ə/ precede vowels
quests.hint: Look for words that end in /ɔː/ or /ə/ and are followed by a vowel.
quests.explanation: “Law” ends in /ɔː/ and “and” begins with a vowel, and “idea” ends in /ə/ with “are” beginning with a vowel. Both are typical sites for an intrusive /r/ in non-rhotic accents. “The law” and “the idea” have a consonant or a different structure before the noun, so no /r/ occurs. Production is optional.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive /r/ occurs after word-final /ə/, /ɑː/ and /ɔː/ before a vowel-initial word in non-rhotic accents.
quests.spokenForm: Pablo, the law-rand the idea-rare clear

quests.instruction: Which /r/ sounds are linking and which are intrusive in “Quinn, there is a banana and a pear”?
quests.word: Quinn, there is a banana and a pear
quests.textToSpeak: Quinn, there is a banana and a pear
options: A linking /r/ in “there is”, and an intrusive /r/ in “banana and”
An intrusive /r/ in “there is”, and a linking /r/ in “banana and”
A linking /r/ in both, because both are in the same sentence
No /r/ in either, in a non-rhotic accent
quests.correctAnswer: A linking /r/ in “there is”, and an intrusive /r/ in “banana and”
quests.hint: Compare the spelling of “there” and “banana” before the vowel-initial words.
quests.explanation: “There” ends in a spelled “r”, so “there is” has a linking /r/. “Banana” ends in /ə/ with no “r” in the spelling, so “banana and” may have an intrusive /r/. In a rhotic accent the first /r/ is pronounced in every position and the second is absent. The distinction depends on both spelling and accent.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking /r/ is present in both rhotic and non-rhotic accents, whereas intrusive /r/ occurs only in non-rhotic accents that use it.
quests.spokenForm: Quinn, there-riz a banana-rand a pear

quests.instruction: Compare “Rafi, drink warm milk” and “Rafi, drink warm cocoa”. Which has a held consonant?
quests.word: Rafi, drink warm milk
quests.textToSpeak: Rafi, drink warm milk
options: “warm cocoa”, where /m/ and /k/ merge into one
Both, because /m/ is held before any consonant
“warm milk”, where two /m/ sounds meet and are held as one
Neither, because gemination needs a vowel between the sounds
quests.correctAnswer: “warm milk”, where two /m/ sounds meet and are held as one
quests.hint: Look for the pair of identical consonants at a boundary.
quests.explanation: In “warm milk” the lips close for the first /m/ and stay closed for the second, giving one longer /m/. In “warm cocoa” the /m/ and /k/ are different sounds and do not merge. Gemination requires two identical consonants side by side. That is how you recognise a held consonant.
quests.phoneticRule: A held (geminate) consonant arises only when two identical consonants meet across a boundary.
quests.spokenForm: Rafi, drink warm-mmilk

quests.instruction: A listener hears one long /k/ in “dark kitchen”. What distinguishes this from elision of a /k/?
quests.word: Umar, the dark kitchen is open
quests.textToSpeak: Umar, the dark kitchen is open
options: The /k/ is longer than a single /k/, because both sounds still contribute to it
The /k/ is shorter than normal, because one /k/ has been removed
The /k/ is replaced by a /g/ that lasts longer
The /k/ is the same length as a single /k/, so it cannot be told apart by ear from a single /k/ in any recording
quests.correctAnswer: The /k/ is longer than a single /k/, because both sounds still contribute to it
quests.hint: Think about how long the consonant lasts compared with a single /k/.
quests.explanation: With gemination the closure is held through the time of both consonants, so you hear one /k/ that is clearly longer than a single one. With elision of one /k/, you would hear a normal-length /k/. The length is therefore the cue. In practice the difference is subtle, but it is audible to a trained ear.
quests.phoneticRule: Geminates are distinguished from single consonants by duration; a held consonant is longer than one produced after elision.
quests.spokenForm: Umar, the dar-kkitchen is open

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “wet towel” fits “Una, use a wet towel”?
quests.word: Una, use a wet towel
quests.textToSpeak: Una, use a wet towel
options: A normal short /t/: “we-towel”, as if one /t/ had been removed from the phrase
Two clear /t/ sounds separated by a short vowel
A /d/ replaces the first /t/ and the second /t/ is kept
One longer /t/: “we-ttowel”, because both /t/ sounds are held as one
quests.correctAnswer: One longer /t/: “we-ttowel”, because both /t/ sounds are held as one
quests.hint: The two /t/ sounds are identical. How long is the closure you hold?
quests.explanation: “Wet” ends in /t/ and “towel” begins with /t/, so the tongue holds one closure and releases once: a longer /t/, “we-ttowel”. A single normal /t/ would suggest that one was omitted. Two clear releases would suggest a careful, separated delivery. The held /t/ is the typical middle path.
quests.phoneticRule: Gemination of /t/ across a boundary yields a single lengthened /t/ with one release.
quests.spokenForm: Una, use a we-ttowel

quests.instruction: What is the difference between “I’ll” and “I will” with a weak “will” in “Vikram, I’ll tell you”?
quests.word: Vikram, I’ll tell you
quests.textToSpeak: Vikram, I’ll tell you
options: “I’ll” and “I will” sound identical in speech
“I’ll” is one syllable, /aɪl/; “I will” with a weak /wɪl/ has two syllables
“I will” is contracted to /aɪl/ whenever it is said at a fast conversational speed
“I’ll” has a stressed /ɪ/ vowel before the /l/
quests.correctAnswer: “I’ll” is one syllable, /aɪl/; “I will” with a weak /wɪl/ has two syllables
quests.hint: Count the syllables in each version when spoken aloud.
quests.explanation: A contraction fuses the pronoun and the auxiliary into one syllable, /aɪl/. A weak form keeps two words, with the second reduced to /wɪl/ or /wəl/. So a full “I will” with weak “will” still has two syllables, while “I’ll” has one. The two are close, but the syllable count separates them.
quests.phoneticRule: A contraction merges two words into one syllable, whereas a weak form reduces a word's vowel but keeps it as a separate syllable.
quests.spokenForm: Vikram, I’ll tel-yuh

quests.instruction: Which of these is a standard contraction and which an informal reduction in “Willa, you’ve got to try this”?
quests.word: Willa, you’ve got to try this
quests.textToSpeak: Willa, you’ve got to try this
options: “you’ve” is an informal reduction; “got to” becoming “gotta” is a standard contraction
“you’ve” is a standard contraction; “got to” becoming “gotta” is an informal reduction
Both are standard contractions found in formal writing
Both are informal reductions that should be avoided in speech
quests.correctAnswer: “you’ve” is a standard contraction; “got to” becoming “gotta” is an informal reduction
quests.hint: Think about which form you could write in an ordinary email and which only in a casual message.
quests.explanation: “You’ve” is a standard contraction of “you have”, accepted in many written contexts. “Gotta” is the informal spoken form of “got to” and belongs mainly to speech and casual writing. Both involve reduction, but they differ in register. Recognising both is part of understanding casual speech.
quests.phoneticRule: Standard contractions are widely accepted, whereas informal reductions such as “gotta” are limited to casual speech and writing.
quests.spokenForm: Willa, you’ve gotta try this

quests.instruction: In “Yan, she’s been waiting”, what does “’s” stand for?
quests.word: Yan, she’s been waiting
quests.textToSpeak: Yan, she’s been waiting
options: “Has”, because “been” is a past participle
“Is”, because “waiting” follows
“Was”, because the sentence is in the past
“Does”, because “been” is a verb
quests.correctAnswer: “Has”, because “been” is a past participle
quests.hint: Look at the verb form that comes straight after the contraction.
quests.explanation: The contracted /z/ can stand for “is” or “has”. Because “been” is a past participle, the sentence needs “has”: “she has been waiting”. The sound /ʃiːz/ is the same in both cases. So, as with “’d”, grammar decides what the contraction stands for.
quests.phoneticRule: Contracted ’s is ambiguous between “is” and “has”; the form of the following verb disambiguates it.
quests.spokenForm: Yan, sheez been waiting

quests.instruction: Which features hide “did you” in “Zeke, what did you do with the keys?”
quests.word: Zeke, what did you do with the keys
quests.textToSpeak: Zeke, what did you do with the keys
options: A /tʃ/ blend in “what did”, and a strong “with”
Elision of the /d/ in “did”, and a strong “you”
Assimilation of the /t/ in “what”, and a /j/ glide
A /dʒ/ blend in “did you”, and weak forms in “with the”
quests.correctAnswer: A /dʒ/ blend in “did you”, and weak forms in “with the”
quests.hint: Say the question fast and listen to what happens to “did you” and to the small words near the end.
quests.explanation: “Did you” blends into /dʒ/, so it sounds like “dija”. “With the” is weak: /wɪð ðə/. The stressed words are “what”, “do” and “keys”. Because the blend and the weak forms are all quiet, the middle of the question is easy to lose. Listening for the stressed words helps you decode the rest.
quests.phoneticRule: In a fast question, coalescence and weak forms hide function words so that only the stressed words stay prominent.
quests.spokenForm: Zeke, wot di-ja do with the keys

quests.instruction: Which features are hidden in “Abel, how long have you been waiting here?”
quests.word: Abel, how long have you been waiting here
quests.textToSpeak: Abel, how long have you been waiting here
options: A /dʒ/ blend in “have you”, and a strong “been”
A weak “have” (/əv/), a weak “you” (/jə/) and a weak “been” (/bɪn/)
Elision of the /v/ in “have”, and a /j/ glide
A linking /r/ in “long have”, a /ʃ/ blend, and a strong “you” in the question
quests.correctAnswer: A weak “have” (/əv/), a weak “you” (/jə/) and a weak “been” (/bɪn/)
quests.hint: Pick out the small words after “long” and say how strong each one is.
quests.explanation: “Have”, “you” and “been” are all function words in this question, so each takes a weak form: /əv/, /jə/ and /bɪn/. “Have you” does not blend, because /v/ is not one of the four triggers. The stressed words are “long” and “waiting”. So the hidden features are three weak forms in a row.
quests.phoneticRule: A run of auxiliary, pronoun and participle is typically weak, producing an unstressed stretch between stressed words.
quests.spokenForm: Abel, how long uv-yuh bin waiting here

quests.instruction: Which spoken form fits “Cora, are you going to be there at nine?”
quests.word: Cora, are you going to be there at nine
quests.textToSpeak: Cora, are you going to be there at nine
options: “are you going to be there at nine”: every word with a full vowel and no linking
“ar-ya gonta be there at nine”: the /t/ of “to” is kept
“are-chu going to be there at nine”: a /tʃ/ blend after “are”
“ar-ya gonna be there at nine”: weak “are you”, “gonna”, and a weak “at”
quests.correctAnswer: “ar-ya gonna be there at nine”: weak “are you”, “gonna”, and a weak “at”
quests.hint: Find the three function-word stretches and decide which of them is weak.
quests.explanation: “Are you” is weak: /ə jə/, with no blend because “are” ends in a vowel. “Going to” is often “gonna”. “At” is weak: /ət/. Stressed words are “there” and “nine”. So the question is easy to say but hard to hear if you expect full forms.
quests.phoneticRule: Weak forms and the informal “gonna” combine in questions about plans, leaving only the key words stressed.
quests.spokenForm: Cora, ar-ya gonna be there at nine

quests.instruction: Which sentence matches the fast “Nico, wot-dja wanna do nex’ week?”
quests.word: Nico, what do you want to do next week
quests.textToSpeak: Nico, what do you want to do next week
options: “Nico, what did you want to do next week?”
“Nico, what do you want to do last week?”
“Nico, what do you want to do next week?”
“Nico, why do you want to do next week?”
quests.correctAnswer: “Nico, what do you want to do next week?”
quests.hint: Decode the stressed words first, then match the reduced stretches to grammar and context.
quests.explanation: “Wot-dja” can stand for “what do you”, “wanna” stands for “want to”, and “nex’ week” has an omitted /t/. The past-tense “did” does not fit the future time reference “next week”. So grammar and context decide between “do” and “did” when the sound is ambiguous.
quests.phoneticRule: Decoding fast speech combines sound cues with grammar and context, especially where blends make two words sound alike.
quests.spokenForm: Nico, wot-dja wanna do nex’ week

quests.instruction: Which sentence matches the fast “Tariq, I dunno if they’re gonna come”?
quests.word: Tariq, I don’t know if they’re going to come
quests.textToSpeak: Tariq, I don’t know if they’re going to come
options: “Tariq, I do know if they’re going to come”
“Tariq, I don’t know if they were going to come”
“Tariq, I didn’t know if they’re going to come”
“Tariq, I don’t know if they’re going to come”
quests.correctAnswer: “Tariq, I don’t know if they’re going to come”
quests.hint: Match “dunno” and “gonna” to their standard sources, then check the tense of the rest.
quests.explanation: “Dunno” stands for “don’t know”, “gonna” for “going to”, and “they’re” is a contraction of “they are”. The other options change the negative, the tense or both. A listener must therefore keep track of both the reductions and the grammar. This is what understanding fast speech means.
quests.phoneticRule: Informal reductions map to standard phrases, and the surrounding tense and polarity must remain consistent with the reduced form.
quests.spokenForm: Tariq, I dunno if they’re gonna come

quests.instruction: In a fast “Una, the next bus left at nine”, which /t/ is most likely to be omitted?
quests.word: Una, the next bus left at nine
quests.textToSpeak: Una, the next bus left at nine
options: The /t/ of “left”, before the vowel of “at”
The /t/ of “next”, before the consonant /b/
The /t/ of “at”, before “nine”
The /b/ of “bus”, at the start of the word
quests.correctAnswer: The /t/ of “next”, before the consonant /b/
quests.hint: Which /t/ is followed by a consonant, and which is followed by a vowel?
quests.explanation: “Next” ends in /kst/ before the consonant /b/, so its /t/ is often omitted: “nex’ bus”. “Left” ends in /ft/ before the vowel of “at”, so its /t/ links onto it. So only one /t/ is a good candidate for omission. Applying the rule boundary by boundary gives the answer.
quests.phoneticRule: Omission is a candidate only where a word-final /t/ is followed by a consonant, not where it is followed by a vowel.
quests.spokenForm: Una, the nex’ bus lef-tat nine

quests.instruction: At a café you say, “Excuse me, could I get a cup of tea?” Which delivery is the most natural?
quests.word: Excuse me, could I get a cup of tea
quests.textToSpeak: Excuse me, could I get a cup of tea
options: Linked and reduced: “cou-dai ge-ta cup-a tea”, with beats on “get” and “tea”
Word by word, with a pause after each word and a full vowel on every one of them
Reduced but unlinked, with every small word dropped
Fully linked but with strong “of” and “a” in every case
quests.correctAnswer: Linked and reduced: “cou-dai ge-ta cup-a tea”, with beats on “get” and “tea”
quests.hint: Imagine a friendly request at a busy counter. Which words carry the beats?
quests.explanation: The natural delivery links “could I” (“cou-dai”), “get a” (“ge-ta”) and “cup of” (“cup-a”), and reduces the small words. The stressed words are “get” and “tea”, with a lighter beat on “could”. A word-by-word delivery is clear but stiff, and dropping the small words changes the grammar.
quests.phoneticRule: A natural request links consonants onto vowel-initial small words and reduces them, while the content words carry the beats.
quests.spokenForm: Excuse me, cou-dai ge-ta cup-a tea

quests.instruction: Why does a fast “Rafi, could you tell me where the station is?” have fewer beats than written words?
quests.word: Rafi, could you tell me where the station is
quests.textToSpeak: Rafi, could you tell me where the station is
options: The speaker drops half of the words to save time on a busy platform
Every word is shortened equally, so no word carries a beat in the question
The beats fall on the small words, which are the loudest in the sentence
Only content words carry beats; small words are blended and squeezed
quests.correctAnswer: Only content words carry beats; small words are blended and squeezed
quests.hint: Imagine the question said at speed, and listen for how many real beats you hear.
quests.explanation: The stressed words are “tell”, “where” and “station”. “Could you” blends into “cou-ja”, “me” and “the” are squeezed, and “is” is weak. So a ten-word question may have only three or four beats. Hearing the beats first lets you decode the rest from context.
quests.phoneticRule: In a long question the number of beats is determined by the content words, so the small words add little to the length.
quests.spokenForm: Rafi, cou-ja tell me where the station is

quests.instruction: Which spoken form fits “Selma, I’ll pick it up on my way”?
quests.word: Selma, I’ll pick it up on my way
quests.textToSpeak: Selma, I’ll pick it up on my way
options: “pi-ki-tup om my way”: linked, with the /n/ shifting to /m/
“pick it up on my way”: five separated words
“pi-kit-up on my way”: with only the first link
“pi-ki-tup-ong my way”: with the /n/ shifting to /ŋ/
quests.correctAnswer: “pi-ki-tup om my way”: linked, with the /n/ shifting to /m/
quests.hint: Mark the consonant + vowel links first, then check the nasal before “my”.
quests.explanation: “Pick it up” links as “pi-ki-tup” (the /k/ onto “it” and the /t/ onto “up”). The /n/ of “on” sits before /m/, so it shifts to [m]: “om my way”. The sentence is therefore a mixture of linking and assimilation. A natural delivery uses both without effort.
quests.phoneticRule: Phrasal-verb chunks link consonants onto following vowels, and a following nasal-plus-lip-sound boundary assimilates.
quests.spokenForm: Selma, I’ll pi-ki-tup om my way

quests.instruction: Which analysis fits “Tariq, bet you ten pounds I got it”?
quests.word: Tariq, bet you ten pounds I got it
quests.textToSpeak: Tariq, bet you ten pounds I got it
options: A /dʒ/ blend, elision of the /n/ and a /j/ glide
A /tʃ/ blend, gemination in “ten pounds” and an intrusive /r/
A /tʃ/ blend (“bet you”), assimilation of /n/ to [m] (“ten pounds”), linking (“got it”)
Elision of the /t/ in “bet you”, assimilation of the /p/ in “pounds” and linking in “got it”
quests.correctAnswer: A /tʃ/ blend (“bet you”), assimilation of /n/ to [m] (“ten pounds”), linking (“got it”)
quests.hint: Take each boundary in turn: /t/ + /j/, /n/ + /p/, and a consonant + vowel.
quests.explanation: “Bet you” has /t/ + /j/, so it blends into /tʃ/. “Ten pounds” has /n/ before the lip sound /p/, so the /n/ shifts to [m]. “Got it” has a /t/ before a vowel, so it links. Each boundary is therefore handled by a different process. That is the skill of the final analysis.
quests.phoneticRule: Each boundary in a complex phrase is analysed independently: /t/ + /j/ gives coalescence, a nasal before a lip sound gives assimilation, and a consonant before a vowel gives linking.
quests.spokenForm: Tariq, be-choo tem pounds I go-tit

quests.instruction: Which analysis fits “Yan, did he say you’ve got to go?”
quests.word: Yan, did he say you’ve got to go
quests.textToSpeak: Yan, did he say you’ve got to go
options: A /dʒ/ blend in “did he”, and a strong “got to”
A dropped /h/ with a link (“did he”), and the informal “gotta” (“got to”)
Assimilation in “did he”, and gemination in “say you’ve”
Elision of the /d/ in “did”, and a /tʃ/ blend in “got to”
quests.correctAnswer: A dropped /h/ with a link (“did he”), and the informal “gotta” (“got to”)
quests.hint: Check whether “he” could trigger a blend, then look at “got to”.
quests.explanation: “He” loses its /h/ after “did”, so the /d/ links onto it: “di-dee”. There is no /j/, so no blend occurs. “Got to” is reduced to “gotta”, an informal form. The sentence thus combines /h/ dropping with linking and an informal reduction.
quests.phoneticRule: A pronoun that loses its /h/ triggers linking rather than coalescence, because it has no /j/; informal reductions are independent of it.
quests.spokenForm: Yan, di-dee say you’ve gotta go

quests.instruction: Which analysis fits “Quinn, I can’t meet you, my best friend is ill”?
quests.word: Quinn, I can’t meet you, my best friend is ill
quests.textToSpeak: Quinn, I can’t meet you, my best friend is ill
options: Elision (“can’t meet”), assimilation (“meet you”), and linking (“best friend”)
Assimilation (“can’t meet”), coalescence (“meet you”), and elision (“best friend”)
Assimilation (“can’t meet”), linking (“meet you”), and gemination (“best friend”)
Coalescence (“can’t meet”), assimilation (“meet you”), and elision (“best friend”)
quests.correctAnswer: Assimilation (“can’t meet”), coalescence (“meet you”), and elision (“best friend”)
quests.hint: Name the next sound at each of the three boundaries and decide what process it triggers.
quests.explanation: “Can’t meet” has /n/ + /m/ with a weak /t/, so the nasal is assimilated: “caam meet”. “Meet you” has /t/ + /j/, so it blends into /tʃ/. “Best friend” has a /t/ between /s/ and /f/, which is often omitted. Three processes appear in one sentence, each determined by its own neighbouring sounds.
quests.phoneticRule: A complex phrase may combine assimilation, coalescence and elision, each triggered by a different neighbouring sound.
quests.spokenForm: Quinn, I caam mee-choo, my bes’ friend is ill
